hull_white_short_rate_model.text: `cox_ingersoll_ross_model` prices a zero-coupon bond and simulates a short rate whose volatility scales with the square root of the rate level, which keeps the rate non-negative. It answers: "what is the bond worth, and how might a non-negative rate evolve?" `hull_white_short_rate_model` uses constant volatility with no square root, so rates can go negative, and it answers the same bond-price question under that simpler dynamic. With a constant `theta_const` it simply calls `vasicek_interest_rate_model`, so it is not a time-dependent fit to a market forward curve. The CIR function requires `theta`, while the Hull-White one takes an optional `theta_const`. The CIR simulation uses the exact transition distribution, so `n_steps` affects only path granularity.

explain.text: `cox_ingersoll_ross_model` (Cox Ingersoll Ross Model) works with the CIR short-rate model, where the rate mean-reverts toward a long-run level `theta` at speed `kappa` and its volatility scales with the square root of the rate, so it stays non-negative. Given `r0`, `kappa`, `theta`, `sigma` and `maturity`, it returns a closed-form zero-coupon bond price. It also simulates short-rate paths by Monte Carlo, using the exact non-central chi-squared transition rather than an Euler approximation. That means `n_steps` only sets path granularity, while `n_simulations` and `seed` control the number of paths and reproducibility.

when.text:
- Use Cox Ingersoll Ross Model when you need this: CIR model: closed-form ZCB price + simulated (non-negative) short rate.
- It takes `r0`, `kappa`, `theta`, `sigma`, `maturity`, `n_steps`. For a different question, compare with `hull_white_short_rate_model` in the same group. It is one of the functions listed on its domain page of the pyvar portal, with a Try it panel.
